introduction-the-green-build-lie.core: Two PRs can each pass CI against an old main and still break main when combined, because neither was tested against the other. A green PR build isn't proof that main will be green.

first_principles.problem: Main breaks several times a week even though every PR was green, blocking everyone.
truths: CI tests a PR against the base at the time it ran.
Semantic conflicts don't show up as Git conflicts.
derivation: Recognise that **PR CI is stale** once main moves.
Test the **exact merge result** before landing.
**Serialise** landings through a queue.
Optimise the queue's **throughput**.

analogy.title: Two editors of a shared doc
analogy.story: One renames a heading while the other adds a reference to the old name. Each edit is fine; together they break the doc.
analogy.breaks: Requiring branches to be up to date before merging works, but forces endless rebases on busy repos.

check.q: How can two green PRs break main?
check.a: Each was tested against an older main without the other's changes, and they conflict semantically.

what-is-a-merge-queue.core: A merge queue lines up approved PRs and, for each one, tests the PR applied on top of the latest main plus everything ahead of it in the queue. Only exact combinations that pass get merged, so main stays green.

first_principles.problem: Manual 'update branch, wait for CI, merge' races don't scale on busy repos.
truths: Main must only receive tested states.
Ordering makes the expected state predictable.
derivation: PR approved → **enters the queue**.
Queue builds a **temporary merge branch** (main + queued PRs + this PR).
CI **passes → fast-forward main**; **fails → eject** the PR.
Next in line continues.

analogy.title: A traffic controller on a single-lane bridge
analogy.story: Cars cross one at a time in order, and each crossing is verified safe.
analogy.breaks: A strictly serial queue is slow when CI is slow, so it needs parallelism or batching.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: B's author is notified, and main never breaks.

check.q: What exactly does a merge queue test?
check.a: The PR combined with the latest main and all PRs ahead of it in the queue.

optimistic-merging-speeding-up-the-line.core: Instead of waiting for each queued PR's CI to finish, start CI for the next ones speculatively, each assuming those ahead will pass. When they do, PRs land in parallel; when one fails, the speculative builds behind it are restarted without it.

first_principles.problem: With 30-minute CI, a serial queue lands only 2 PRs per hour.
truths: Speculation is cheap when it's usually right.
derivation: Build **main+A**, **main+A+B** and **main+A+B+C** at once.
If all pass, **land all**.
If B fails, **eject B** and rebuild C on main+A.
Tune the **queue depth** to CI capacity.

analogy.title: A kitchen cooking several orders at once
analogy.story: Start the next dishes before the first is plated, assuming no order gets cancelled.
analogy.breaks: A high failure rate wastes compute on discarded speculative builds.

example.title: Throughput comparison
example.outcome: the queue keeps up with a busy team.

check.q: What happens to speculative builds behind a failed PR?
check.a: They're discarded and restarted without the failed PR.

batching-strategies-bors-ng-tide.core: Batching tests several queued PRs together in one CI run. If the batch passes, all of them land. If it fails, bisect the batch to find the culprit, which saves CI cost when test suites are very slow.

first_principles.problem: One-hour test suites make even parallel per-PR CI expensive and slow.
truths: Most PRs pass, so most batches pass.
One run can validate many PRs.
Bisection isolates failures in log₂(n) runs.
derivation: Combine **N PRs** into one merge candidate.
**Pass → land all N**.
**Fail → split** the batch in half and retest.
Pick a **batch size** based on the failure rate.

analogy.title: Group-testing blood samples
analogy.story: Pool ten samples; if the pool is clean, all ten are clean. If not, split and retest.
analogy.breaks: Flaky tests poison batches and cause needless bisection.

linear-history-vs-merge-commits.core: A merge queue can land changes by merge commit (preserves branch structure), squash (one commit per PR) or rebase (linear individual commits). Linear history makes bisect and reading easier; merge commits keep context.

first_principles.problem: Inconsistent landing styles make history hard to read and bisect.
truths: History is read for debugging and audits.
Bisect works best when every commit builds.
derivation: **Squash**: one clean commit per PR (most common).
**Rebase**: linear, but every commit must build.
**Merge commit**: true topology, noisier history.
Pick **one policy** and enforce it.

analogy.title: A book's chapters vs. a draft's revision trail
analogy.story: Squash gives clean chapters; merge commits keep every editing session's trail.
analogy.breaks: Squash loses intermediate commits, which matters if they were meaningful.

check.q: Why does squash merging help git bisect?
check.a: Every commit on main corresponds to a full tested PR, so each one builds and passes.

merge-queue-implementations-in-practice.core: GitHub's merge queue (native, required checks on merge_group events), GitLab merge trains (pipelines on the combined ref) and third-party tools like Mergify or Bors all implement the same idea with different configuration and features.

first_principles.problem: Knowing the theory isn't enough. Each platform needs specific setup, such as CI triggering on the queue's events.
truths: CI must run on the queue's temporary refs.
derivation: **GitHub**: enable the merge queue in branch rules, and trigger CI on **merge_group**.
**GitLab**: enable **merge trains**.
**Mergify/Bors**: config file rules, batching and priorities.
Set **required checks** and **concurrency**.

analogy.title: Different brands of traffic lights
analogy.story: Same principle, different wiring for each city.
analogy.breaks: Forgetting the merge_group trigger leaves the queue waiting forever for checks.
